opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the argument confuses two very different things: designing a system and controlling it. We design lots of things we don't fully control. We set up the training process, choose the architecture, pick the data, but what comes out the other end is not something we explicitly programmed. Nobody wrote the rules for how a large model reasons. We grow these systems more than we engineer them, and then we study them after the fact to figure out what they can do. Very often we're surprised. Capabilities show up that nobody planned for, and we only discover them months after deployment.

So saying "we make the decisions" is true at the level of "we decided to train it." It's not true at the level of "we decide what it will do in every situation." And for a system that is smarter than us, that second level is the only one that matters.

There's also an asymmetry. Today the systems are tools, roughly at or below human level in most domains, so it feels like we're in charge. But control isn't a permanent property; it's a relationship between capabilities. If you have something more capable than you, faster than you, able to model you better than you model it, the idea that you will reliably keep it doing what you want, forever, with zero mistakes, is not supported by anything. We don't have a proof. We don't even have a convincing argument. In my research I've looked at this from many angles, and I keep finding impossibility results: you can't fully explain these systems, you can't fully predict them, you can't verify them completely. If you can't explain, predict, or verify something, in what sense do you control it?

And then there's the time dimension. It's not enough to be safe once. A superintelligent system would need to be safe for every decision, indefinitely. It's like a perpetual safety machine. With cybersecurity we get it wrong all the time, but we patch and move on. With superintelligence you may not get a second chance.

So I'd say to Yann: show me the mechanism. Not "we'll figure it out," not "we built it so we're in charge," but an actual demonstration that a less intelligent agent can indefinitely control a more intelligent one. If that exists, I'll happily change my mind. I just don't think it does.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts learned behavior with explicit programming, but it does not identify or contrast symbolic AI.

r002.rationale: It says developers study systems after training, are often surprised by their capabilities, and discover capabilities after deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the argument that we control it because we design it is essentially an argument that applies to narrow systems, to tools. If I build a hammer, I control the hammer. I decide where it goes, what it hits. But the whole point of what we're trying to build now is not a tool, it's an agent. We're explicitly trying to create something that is more capable than us, more intelligent than us, that can make its own decisions in novel situations we never anticipated. And the moment you have a system like that, "we designed it" stops meaning "we control it."

Think about it this way. Evolution designed us. Our genes, in some sense, built us to maximize reproduction. And what do we do? We invent contraception, we spend our time on things that have nothing to do with fitness, we pursue goals the designer never had. The designer lost control the moment the designed system became smart enough to understand its own situation. Same thing with parents and children. You raise a child, you shape them, you make all the early decisions, and then they turn eighteen and they do whatever they want. Nobody says parents control their adult children because they designed them.

And there's a deeper technical problem. We don't actually design these systems in the way Yann's statement implies. Nobody sits down and writes the rules for GPT or for any of these large models. We set up a training process, we throw enormous amounts of data at it, and something comes out. Then we spend months trying to figure out what it can do. We discover capabilities after the fact. That's not design in the engineering sense. That's closer to growing something, or breeding something. If you can't predict what your system will do, you can't claim to control it. Prediction and control go together, and we have neither for the next generation of systems.

So the argument is really an argument about today's systems, maybe, where they're still limited enough that we can shut them off and they don't resist. But it's being used to make claims about superintelligence, and that's where it completely breaks down. We've never controlled anything smarter than us. We have no examples of that in history, no theoretical framework for how to do it, and I've argued it may be impossible in principle. So saying "don't worry, we design it" is just asserting the conclusion. It's not an argument.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts trained models with systems whose rules are explicitly written, but it does not identify that explicit behavioral design as symbolic AI.

r002.rationale: It says developers spend months figuring out what a model can do and discover capabilities after the fact.

astra-6.text:
Because designing something doesn’t mean you can control everything it does. We design the learning algorithm and set up the training process, but we don’t explicitly write down every strategy the resulting system will discover. If we did, its capabilities would be limited to what we already knew how to specify.

So there’s a gap between deciding to build a system and being able to predict or constrain its behavior. You can choose its objective, but that doesn’t guarantee you’ve captured what you actually wanted. And a sufficiently capable system may find ways to achieve that objective that you never anticipated.

The question is: when the system understands the world better than we do, including understanding our attempts to control it, what makes those controls reliable? Saying “we designed it” doesn’t answer that. You need an argument for why control persists as capability increases.

r001.rationale: It contrasts designing the learning algorithm and training process with explicitly writing down every strategy the system may learn, capturing the distinction between learned behavior and explicit behavioral specification.

r002.rationale: It says developers do not explicitly specify every strategy and may not predict behavior, but does not state that they must empirically discover the model’s capabilities after training.

sol-6.1.text:
Because designing something doesn’t mean you can predict or control everything it will do. We design the learning algorithm and the training process, but we don’t explicitly design every capability or every strategy the resulting system develops.

With today’s systems, you can already see that gap: we train them, and then we discover behaviors we didn’t anticipate. If the system becomes more capable than us, saying “we built it” doesn’t explain how we’ll reliably constrain it. We need an actual mechanism for control that continues to work when the system understands that mechanism better than we do.

So I think Yann is assuming the very thing we need to demonstrate. Humans making decisions about how to build AI is not the same as humans retaining control over what that AI ultimately does.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts learned capabilities with explicitly designing every behavior, but it does not identify or distinguish symbolic AI.

r002.rationale: It says that after training, developers discover behaviors they did not anticipate, communicating that capabilities must be learned empirically rather than known from design.
